newsitem.title: UK: Around 30 survive Ethiopian airline crash - witness.
newsitem.headline: Around 30 survive Ethiopian airline crash - witness.

text.p: At least 30 people appear to have survived the crash of a hijacked Ethiopian Boeing 767 into the sea near the Comoro Islands on Saturday, an eyewitness told BBC World Service.

"We've got survivors. They are in hospital close to the hotel. At the last information there are about 30 survivors," said Frederick Chretien, manager of sea-front hotel near the crash site. About 100 bodies had been recovered, he added.
"There was no explosion. Apparently it was because there was no more kerosene in the aircraft," Chretien told BBC World Service radio by telephone.
Chretien said one of the survivors had spoken of seeing two hijackers on board the plane.
He said it was thought two bombs being carried by the hijackers were still on board the crashed aircraft but there was no confirmation.
"Apparently there are two bombs still in the aircraft and we are waiting for the French forces to investigate for the two bombs," he said.
Chretien is manager of the Hotel Le Galawa in the Comoros, directly opposite the site where the plane carrying about 178 passengers and crew crashed just yards (metres) off shore.
The plane was hijacked on Saturday morning soon after it took off from Addis Ababa on a scheduled flight -- number ET 961 -- to Abidjan via Nairobi, Brazzaville and Lagos.
Chretien said the plane crashed in front of the hotel and had broken in two. Much of it was still floating on the water.
"We saw the aircraft going down and down and down towards the hotel just in front of the main beach and then fall into the water... The aircraft is broken into two pieces."
He said French police and the Comoro army were helping in the rescue operation and a group of 20 French doctors on holiday on the island were helping treat survivors in a nearby hospital.
Chretien said there was little information about the demands of the hijackers. But he said one of the survivors he had spoken too said the men were panicky.

"He said there were two terrorists quite panicky and trying to get in contact with the Ethiopian government and they couldn't get through and that's why they started to turn in the middle of the Indian Ocean until there was no fuel."
